.@elonmusk on the future of energy and intelligence. 

"As you harness more and more of the Sun's energy, the ability to turn that into intelligence is fundamentally a digital computer thing."

Musk points out how enormous the Sun's energy supply really is.

Even if civilization increased its total energy use by 1 million times, it would still use far less than one-millionth of the Sun's energy.

Most of that future energy use would likely happen in deep space.

The bigger idea:

Humanity's future may be about turning more of the Sun's enormous energy supply into computation, AI, and intelligence.

From solar energy to digital intelligence.

Video

Elon Musk on the future of SpaceXAI. 

"The future is fundamentally AI and robots."

Musk says SpaceXAI's AI revenue could surpass all other SpaceX revenue as early as September.

He expects AI revenue to become significantly larger than SpaceX's other businesses in Q4.

That's why he says succeeding in AI—both hardware and software—is now vital to SpaceXAI's future.

And Musk sees the long-term shift as much bigger than just AI becoming smarter.

He believes digital intelligence could eventually become billions or even trillions of times greater than biological intelligence.

The future, according to Musk, is AI, robots, and digital intelligence at an unimaginable scale.

Video

Elon Musk on the incredible scale of Starship. 

"Hard to believe that humans made such a thing. I think the future will look back and say, 'Not bad for a bunch of humans.'"

Musk says Starship could completely transform humanity's ability to move mass into space.

Today, humanity puts roughly 2,500 tonnes into orbit each year.

With Starship, Musk believes that could rise to more than 1 million tonnes per year—and potentially approach 10 million tonnes.

Those numbers sound almost impossible.

But Musk says that's the kind of scale required to build a sustainable civilization on the Moon, Mars, and beyond.

"If you can't deliver millions of tons to Earth orbit, you can't get the millions of tons you need to the Moon and Mars."

He calls Starship arguably one of the hardest engineering projects humanity has ever attempted.

And the team is pushing forward across engines, avionics, structures, and launch operations.

The goal isn't just a bigger rocket.

It's the infrastructure for a multiplanetary civilization. 🌍→🌙→🔴

Video

Elon Musk on Starshield's growing role in national security. 

"Starshield has become a vital part of national security."

Musk says SpaceX can't reveal too much about the program because of its highly sensitive nature.

But he praised the Starshield team for their work and highlighted how important the system has become to America's national security.

Another major milestone for SpaceX—this time beyond commercial spaceflight.

Video

Elon Musk on the future of @Starlink and internet traffic. 

"Today, we're in 167 countries, with 22 million mobile subscribers and 13 million high-bandwidth subscribers."

Musk expects those numbers to grow by more than 10× over time.

But the bigger shift could come from AI.

Musk referenced Cloudflare's projection that, based on current growth, AI traffic could eventually become 1,000× larger than human internet traffic within five years.

Think about that for a moment.

The internet of the future may not be dominated by humans talking to each other.

It could be dominated by AI systems talking to AI systems.

Video

Elon Musk on how Starlink grew from nothing into a global internet network. 

"If you've got a rocket that can fly a lot, what do you fly on it?"

That question helped lead to Starlink.

Musk says the Starlink team built a high-bandwidth global internet system from scratch, both the hardware and the software.

Today, Starlink has nearly 11,000 satellites in orbit, more than twice as many as everyone else combined.

And Musk believes Starlink could eventually handle more than 90% of global internet traffic.

With Starlink V3 and beyond, the network could eventually scale to around 100,000 satellites.

Building an entire internet network in space is an enormous challenge.

But SpaceX is already doing it.

Elon Musk reveals why he launched his Tesla Roadster into space. 

"I fully expected this flight to fail."

Musk was talking about Falcon Heavy's first flight.

Since he thought the rocket might fail, he didn't want to put something boring on top of it.

Instead, SpaceX launched his personal Tesla Roadster with Starman sitting in the driver's seat.

The car is now traveling in an orbit that takes it between Earth and Mars.

And according to Musk, it could remain up there for around 10 million years.

Imagine taking your everyday car and accidentally turning it into a piece of space history.

Elon Musk reflects on how difficult SpaceX's journey really was. 

"When we started SpaceX, we really had no idea how to make rockets."

Falcon 1 failed three times before finally reaching orbit.

Then came an even bigger challenge: landing and re-flying an orbital booster.

Musk says many aerospace experts told him it wouldn't work—and even if it did, nobody would want to fly on a used rocket.

But SpaceX kept going.

Today, Falcon 9 boosters take off, land, and get recovered every few days.

SpaceX also went on to build Falcon Heavy, once the world's most powerful operational rocket, and is now approaching its 700th Falcon flight.

From blowing up rockets to routinely landing and reusing them.

That's what years of iteration look like.

Video

Elon Musk on SpaceX's Dragon spacecraft. 

Dragon became the first privately developed spacecraft to reach and communicate with the International Space Station.

It also became the first commercial spacecraft to carry astronauts.

Since then, Dragon has flown dozens of missions, including crewed flights and asteroid missions.

So far, SpaceX says Dragon has carried 78 crew members.

Musk believes it won't be long before that number passes 100.

"Dragon has been an amazing vehicle."

A huge milestone for commercial spaceflight—and another chapter in SpaceX's journey.

Video

Elon Musk looking back at SpaceX's early days: 🚀

"All of SpaceX in the beginning was just a small warehouse in El Segundo."

From a tiny warehouse to one of the world's most ambitious space companies.

A powerful reminder that massive companies can start from surprisingly humble beginnings.

Video

Elon Musk on the future of SpaceX and humanity: 

"The mission is to make life multi-planetary, to extend consciousness beyond Earth and understand the universe."

Musk says one of the most inspiring futures imaginable is a civilization spread across the stars.

A future where humanity explores other planets, reaches other star systems, meets alien civilizations, or even discovers the ruins of civilizations that existed millions of years ago.

And that's what he says gets him excited to wake up in the morning.

Life can't just be about solving one problem after another.

There have to be things that make us look forward to the future.

"For me, being a spacefaring civilization is the most interesting thing we could possibly do for the future."

"Making Star Trek real."

Video

Elon Musk on the risks of AI:

"If AI is a potential risk to the public, then there should be some regulatory body that oversees what companies are doing."

Musk argues that AI should have regulatory oversight similar to aircraft, cars, and food and drugs, essentially, a referee to make sure companies don't cut corners when developing potentially dangerous technology.

He also pointed to the possibility of artificial superintelligence arriving much sooner than many people expect, with Ray Kurzweil predicting it could happen as early as 2029.

The bigger question isn't whether AI will become incredibly powerful.

It's whether we'll build the right safeguards before it does.

Video

Elon Musk on how technology changes civilization:

"I think technology is the thing that causes these big step changes in civilization."

He compares the internet to the Gutenberg press.

Before the printing press, books were extremely rare. Even if you had a thirst for knowledge, there simply weren't enough books to access.

But the internet changed everything.

Musk described the internet as humanity developing a "nervous system."

Before the internet, information mostly traveled from one person to another. Access was limited.

Now, almost anyone can access almost all of humanity's information from anywhere.

You could be in the middle of the Amazon jungle with a Starlink terminal and potentially have access to more information than the U.S. president had in 1980.

Technology doesn't just give us new tools.

It changes how civilization itself works.

Elon Musk on why he bought Twitter and why free speech matters:

"I think we need to be very cautious about anything that results in the suppression of free speech."

Musk argues that one of the biggest dangers is creating an environment where people feel they can't question certain ideas, even questioning them becomes unacceptable.

He compares this to cancel culture, saying he has faced attempts to cancel him from both the left and the right.

Musk also emphasized why free speech is so important:

"Free speech is actually extremely important."

He pointed to the First Amendment and why it exists in the first place: people came to America from countries where speaking freely could get you imprisoned.

His broader message is simple:

A society cannot remain free if people are afraid to question ideas or speak openly.
